sentences.text: The mill was less than she expected and much more.
She had imagined a building.

What was there, at the bottom of the slope where the river turned, was a rectangle of walls about waist high, full of elder, with one gable end standing to about her shoulder and a doorway in it with the lintel still across the top.
The river went past it fast and shallow and busy, as though it had been let off.
The boar walked into the rectangle through the doorway.
That was the thing that undid her.
Not the road, not the hedges, not the walking through pines that were not there when the road was.
It was that he had the whole of a wall-less ruin available to him on three sides, and he went in through the door.
He stood in the middle of the floor for a while.
Sabela sat down on the wall about six metres away, because her legs had decided.
She had the sense, sitting there in the smell of elder and cold water at half past eleven at night, that she had understood something and would spend a while catching up to it.
He was not lost.
That was the first part.
Everybody who had ever half-seen him crossing a field at dusk had assumed he was wandering, because that is what a big animal in the wrong place looks like from a car.
He was not wandering.
He was commuting.
And the second part, which took her longer, and which she only got hold of properly on the walk home in the dark: the road was still there.
It had never gone anywhere.
Roads are not made of the surface; the surface is just the part people maintain.
The cut into the bank was still cut.
The gradient was still graded.

Somebody in about 1740 had chosen that line down that hill because it was the line that worked, and the choosing was still true, and the hedges and the pine plantation and the wire fence were all things that had been laid on top of a fact.
The boar was not remembering the road.
The boar was just using it, the way you use a thing that is there, and everybody else had stopped being able to see it.
She got home at ten past one.
Her grandfather was in the kitchen with the light on, not making a fuss about it, doing the crossword he had already finished.
"Well?" he said.
"It goes in through the door," said Sabela.
Her grandfather put the pen down and looked at her for a moment, and then he laughed — one short surprised laugh, not at her — and he said, "Does it.
Does it now."
